source_packet.selected_slice: Under the retained circular, when must an SFC-authorised fund be treated as a complex product for distribution? Distinguish mandatory classification, discretionary designation, exclusions and missing classification evidence.

units.text: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has observed that investment funds may, for asset allocation and yield enhancement purposes, gain exposure to private credit and private equity (collectively, private market assets) via: direct exposure through investments in bank or non-bank direct lending in the form of loans or equities to unlisted companies (direct exposure)1; or indirect exposures2 including through investments in business development companies (BDCs)3, collateralised loan obligations (CLOs)4 or financial derivative instruments5.

This circular provides guidance to management companies of funds that are authorised by the SFC for offering to the public in Hong Kong (Funds)6 in this regard. Funds with direct or indirect exposure to private market assets are required to observe the enhanced disclosure requirements set out in this circular. A Fund may be subject to enhanced scrutiny by the SFC in some cases and be classified as a complex product for distribution, where appropriate.

Direct investment in private market assets generally carries higher inherent risks than publicly listed securities, as these assets are typically illiquid, hard to value, and subject to limited regulatory oversight; they also have higher credit risks and thus higher risk of default. While indirect exposures to the private market assets may not present the same level of risk as direct investments, recent market developments have raised concerns about these indirect exposures, such as the rising default risks of underlying investments for private credit funds, widening price-to-NAV discount for listed BDCs, etc. In addition, certain indirect exposures may lack transparency about the underlying private market assets, as they involve layered structures or complex financial instruments such that retail investors may not reasonably understand the features and risks of these indirect exposures.

Considering that retail investors in Hong Kong may have limited familiarity with private market assets and their associated risks, fund managers should ensure that investors are provided with a clear, sufficiently complete and balanced picture of the characteristics, nature and extent of risks associated with various types of exposures a Fund may have to private market assets. Fund managers should also, among other things, ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market of their Funds.
Enhanced disclosure in offering documents
If a Fund may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, its fund manager should ensure that the Fund’s offering document (including the key facts statement (KFS)) clearly discloses:

(i)        the extent and the means of access of exposure (eg, up to [x]% of the Fund’s NAV is invested in listed BDCs which primarily invest in private market assets; [x – y%] of the Fund’s NAV will gain exposure to private loans via investment in senior tranche of CLOs);

(ii)       the nature and characteristics of the underlying private market assets (eg, the minimum credit rating of the CLOs in which the Fund invests, TRSs on an index comprising unsecuritised broadly syndicated loans); and

(iii)      in the offering documents (and where appropriate, the KFS), the key risks associated with the Fund’s exposure to the specific types of private market assets it directly or indirectly invests in, including the impact and implications to the Fund and its investors (e.g. the limited liquidity and lack of transparency of the underlying private market assets of the BDCs can make them more challenging to value, and these valuation uncertainties may negatively impact the BDC’s NAV and hence the Fund’s NAV).
Complex product designation

A Fund will be considered as a complex product if its total direct and indirect exposures to private market assets amount to 50% or more of the Fund’s NAV. On a case-by-case basis, the SFC may also designate a Fund as a complex product, taking into account factors including, without limitation:
•        the aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets of the Fund;
•        the Fund's overall investment strategy, portfolio composition, and liquidity and/or risk profile;

•        the extent, nature and characteristics of the specific asset types in which the Fund invests (eg, the tranches and credit ratings of CLOs; the structure, tranches and underlying assets of SRTs); and
•        any distribution restrictions, requirements or other conditions as may be imposed by the Fund’s home regulators.
In assessing whether the complex product designation is warranted7, the SFC will adopt a holistic approach taking into account the specific circumstances of the case.

A Fund classified as a complex product will be subject to the SFC’s prevailing requirements for the sale of complex products8 including but not limited to ensuring the suitability of the Fund for its investors irrespective of whether solicitation or recommendation is involved.
Target market identification and distributor selection

The SFC wishes to remind fund managers to observe the requirements set out in the “Circular to Product Providers of SFC-authorized unit trusts and mutual funds, SFC-authorized investment-linked assurance schemes and SFC-authorized unlisted structured investment products – Guidance on Internal Product Approval Process”9, which outlines, among others, the requirements regarding target market identification and distributor selection for SFC-authorised funds.

Fund managers should carefully identify the target market to ensure that the Fund, including its underlying investments and associated risks, would be generally understood by the target market and that the Fund’s investment objectives and risk/return profile match the needs and risk appetite of the target market. They should also ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market identified, have the necessary product knowledge to understand the Fund (including whether the Fund is a complex product) and to assign an appropriate product risk rating (if applicable) for the Fund, and advise investors accordingly.

Fund managers are further reminded that the marketing materials of SFC-authorised funds must comply with the Advertising Guidelines Applicable to Collective Investment Schemes Authorized under the Product Codes10, which provide, among other requirements, that advertisements of a Fund should be fair and present a balanced picture of the Fund with adequate risk disclosures.
Others

When seeking the SFC’s authorisation for any new funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, the fund may be subject to the SFC’s closer scrutiny. In some cases, the SFC may not process the fund under the Fund Authorisation Simple Track (FASTrack).

For existing SFC-authorised funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, fund managers are expected to undertake a review of their funds, take appropriate actions including updating the Fund’s offering documents as soon as practicable, and ensure necessary and proper communications with the distributors in light of the guidance provided under this circular (in particular, with respect to paragraphs 9 and 10 above). Fund managers are encouraged to consult the SFC at the earliest opportunity if they are in doubt regarding complex product classification of their Funds.
If you wish to seek clarification of any aspects of this circular, please contact the relevant case officers in charge.
Investment Products Division
Securities and Futures Commission
1 Direct investments in/exposures to private assets fall within the investment limit of 15% of a Fund’s total net asset value (NAV) under 7.3 of the Code on Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds (UT Code).
2 The examples of indirect exposures set out in paragraph 1 above are non-exhaustive, and subject to review and update by the SFC from time to time in view of market developments.
3 BDCs are close-ended funds registered under the US Investment Company Act of 1940, which primarily invest in debt and equity of small and mid-sized companies in the US.
4 CLOs are securities backed by a pool of debt, typically leveraged loans and broadly syndicated loans, or direct lending to unlisted companies.

claims.action: Consult the SFC about doubtful classification
conditions: Managers are in doubt regarding their Funds' complex-product classification.
claims.statement: Managers are encouraged, rather than expressly required, to consult the SFC when classification is doubtful.

evidence.quote: Fund managers are encouraged to consult the SFC at the earliest opportunity if they are in doubt regarding complex product classification of their Funds.

conditions: Direct investments in or exposures to private assets.
claims.statement: Direct private-asset investments or exposures fall within the separate 15% NAV limit under UT Code paragraph 7.3; the circular's complex-product threshold aggregates direct and indirect exposures.

evidence.quote: Direct investments in/exposures to private assets fall within the investment limit of 15% of a Fund’s total net asset value (NAV) under 7.3 of the Code on Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds (UT Code).

uncertainty: The full scope and qualifications of UT Code paragraph 7.3 are not supplied.

temporal: Review and update from time to time.
claims.statement: Indirect-exposure examples are non-exhaustive and may be reviewed and updated by the SFC as markets develop.

evidence.quote: The examples of indirect exposures set out in paragraph 1 above are non-exhaustive, and subject to review and update by the SFC from time to time in view of market developments.

uncertainty: No subsequent updates are supplied.

claims.statement: BDCs are described as US Investment Company Act of 1940 registered close-ended funds primarily investing in debt and equity of small and mid-sized US companies.

evidence.quote: BDCs are close-ended funds registered under the US Investment Company Act of 1940, which primarily invest in debt and equity of small and mid-sized companies in the US.

claims.statement: CLOs are debt-pool-backed securities, typically involving leveraged or broadly syndicated loans, or direct lending to unlisted companies.

evidence.quote: CLOs are securities backed by a pool of debt, typically leveraged loans and broadly syndicated loans, or direct lending to unlisted companies.

claims.statement: Derivative exposure examples include the specified TRSs and SRTs.

evidence.quote: For example, Total Return Swaps on indices with exposure to leveraged loans or broadly syndicated loans (TRSs), or Significant Risk Transfers with underlying assets that are corporate loans (SRTs).

uncertainty: Naming an instrument type alone does not establish a particular Fund's aggregate exposure or classification.

source_packet.selected_slice: Under the retained circular, when must an SFC-authorised fund be treated as a complex product for distribution? Distinguish mandatory classification, discretionary designation, exclusions and missing classification evidence.

units.text: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has observed that investment funds may, for asset allocation and yield enhancement purposes, gain exposure to private credit and private equity (collectively, private market assets) via: direct exposure through investments in bank or non-bank direct lending in the form of loans or equities to unlisted companies (direct exposure)1; or indirect exposures2 including through investments in business development companies (BDCs)3, collateralised loan obligations (CLOs)4 or financial derivative instruments5.

This circular provides guidance to management companies of funds that are authorised by the SFC for offering to the public in Hong Kong (Funds)6 in this regard. Funds with direct or indirect exposure to private market assets are required to observe the enhanced disclosure requirements set out in this circular. A Fund may be subject to enhanced scrutiny by the SFC in some cases and be classified as a complex product for distribution, where appropriate.

Direct investment in private market assets generally carries higher inherent risks than publicly listed securities, as these assets are typically illiquid, hard to value, and subject to limited regulatory oversight; they also have higher credit risks and thus higher risk of default. While indirect exposures to the private market assets may not present the same level of risk as direct investments, recent market developments have raised concerns about these indirect exposures, such as the rising default risks of underlying investments for private credit funds, widening price-to-NAV discount for listed BDCs, etc. In addition, certain indirect exposures may lack transparency about the underlying private market assets, as they involve layered structures or complex financial instruments such that retail investors may not reasonably understand the features and risks of these indirect exposures.

Considering that retail investors in Hong Kong may have limited familiarity with private market assets and their associated risks, fund managers should ensure that investors are provided with a clear, sufficiently complete and balanced picture of the characteristics, nature and extent of risks associated with various types of exposures a Fund may have to private market assets. Fund managers should also, among other things, ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market of their Funds.
Enhanced disclosure in offering documents
If a Fund may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, its fund manager should ensure that the Fund’s offering document (including the key facts statement (KFS)) clearly discloses:

(i)        the extent and the means of access of exposure (eg, up to [x]% of the Fund’s NAV is invested in listed BDCs which primarily invest in private market assets; [x – y%] of the Fund’s NAV will gain exposure to private loans via investment in senior tranche of CLOs);

(ii)       the nature and characteristics of the underlying private market assets (eg, the minimum credit rating of the CLOs in which the Fund invests, TRSs on an index comprising unsecuritised broadly syndicated loans); and

(iii)      in the offering documents (and where appropriate, the KFS), the key risks associated with the Fund’s exposure to the specific types of private market assets it directly or indirectly invests in, including the impact and implications to the Fund and its investors (e.g. the limited liquidity and lack of transparency of the underlying private market assets of the BDCs can make them more challenging to value, and these valuation uncertainties may negatively impact the BDC’s NAV and hence the Fund’s NAV).
Complex product designation

A Fund will be considered as a complex product if its total direct and indirect exposures to private market assets amount to 50% or more of the Fund’s NAV. On a case-by-case basis, the SFC may also designate a Fund as a complex product, taking into account factors including, without limitation:
•        the aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets of the Fund;
•        the Fund's overall investment strategy, portfolio composition, and liquidity and/or risk profile;

•        the extent, nature and characteristics of the specific asset types in which the Fund invests (eg, the tranches and credit ratings of CLOs; the structure, tranches and underlying assets of SRTs); and
•        any distribution restrictions, requirements or other conditions as may be imposed by the Fund’s home regulators.
In assessing whether the complex product designation is warranted7, the SFC will adopt a holistic approach taking into account the specific circumstances of the case.

A Fund classified as a complex product will be subject to the SFC’s prevailing requirements for the sale of complex products8 including but not limited to ensuring the suitability of the Fund for its investors irrespective of whether solicitation or recommendation is involved.
Target market identification and distributor selection

The SFC wishes to remind fund managers to observe the requirements set out in the “Circular to Product Providers of SFC-authorized unit trusts and mutual funds, SFC-authorized investment-linked assurance schemes and SFC-authorized unlisted structured investment products – Guidance on Internal Product Approval Process”9, which outlines, among others, the requirements regarding target market identification and distributor selection for SFC-authorised funds.

Fund managers should carefully identify the target market to ensure that the Fund, including its underlying investments and associated risks, would be generally understood by the target market and that the Fund’s investment objectives and risk/return profile match the needs and risk appetite of the target market. They should also ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market identified, have the necessary product knowledge to understand the Fund (including whether the Fund is a complex product) and to assign an appropriate product risk rating (if applicable) for the Fund, and advise investors accordingly.

Fund managers are further reminded that the marketing materials of SFC-authorised funds must comply with the Advertising Guidelines Applicable to Collective Investment Schemes Authorized under the Product Codes10, which provide, among other requirements, that advertisements of a Fund should be fair and present a balanced picture of the Fund with adequate risk disclosures.
Others

When seeking the SFC’s authorisation for any new funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, the fund may be subject to the SFC’s closer scrutiny. In some cases, the SFC may not process the fund under the Fund Authorisation Simple Track (FASTrack).

For existing SFC-authorised funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, fund managers are expected to undertake a review of their funds, take appropriate actions including updating the Fund’s offering documents as soon as practicable, and ensure necessary and proper communications with the distributors in light of the guidance provided under this circular (in particular, with respect to paragraphs 9 and 10 above). Fund managers are encouraged to consult the SFC at the earliest opportunity if they are in doubt regarding complex product classification of their Funds.
If you wish to seek clarification of any aspects of this circular, please contact the relevant case officers in charge.
Investment Products Division
Securities and Futures Commission
1 Direct investments in/exposures to private assets fall within the investment limit of 15% of a Fund’s total net asset value (NAV) under 7.3 of the Code on Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds (UT Code).
2 The examples of indirect exposures set out in paragraph 1 above are non-exhaustive, and subject to review and update by the SFC from time to time in view of market developments.
3 BDCs are close-ended funds registered under the US Investment Company Act of 1940, which primarily invest in debt and equity of small and mid-sized companies in the US.
4 CLOs are securities backed by a pool of debt, typically leveraged loans and broadly syndicated loans, or direct lending to unlisted companies.
5 For example, Total Return Swaps on indices with exposure to leveraged loans or broadly syndicated loans (TRSs), or Significant Risk Transfers with underlying assets that are corporate loans (SRTs).

6 Except for listed closed-ended alternative asset funds (LAFs). For LAFs, please refer to the circular on LAFs: https://apps.sfc.hk/edistributionWeb/gateway/EN/circular/products/product-authorization/doc?refNo=25EC9
7 In cases where the Fund’s aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets are less than 50% of the Fund’s NAV.

8 Paragraph 5.5 of the SFC’s Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the Securities and Futures Commission and Chapter 6 of the SFC’s Guidelines on Online Distribution and Advisory Platforms, and the relevant Frequently Asked Questions.

source_packet.selected_slice: Under the retained circular, when must an SFC-authorised fund be treated as a complex product for distribution? Distinguish mandatory classification, discretionary designation, exclusions and missing classification evidence.

units.text: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has observed that investment funds may, for asset allocation and yield enhancement purposes, gain exposure to private credit and private equity (collectively, private market assets) via: direct exposure through investments in bank or non-bank direct lending in the form of loans or equities to unlisted companies (direct exposure)1; or indirect exposures2 including through investments in business development companies (BDCs)3, collateralised loan obligations (CLOs)4 or financial derivative instruments5.

This circular provides guidance to management companies of funds that are authorised by the SFC for offering to the public in Hong Kong (Funds)6 in this regard. Funds with direct or indirect exposure to private market assets are required to observe the enhanced disclosure requirements set out in this circular. A Fund may be subject to enhanced scrutiny by the SFC in some cases and be classified as a complex product for distribution, where appropriate.

Direct investment in private market assets generally carries higher inherent risks than publicly listed securities, as these assets are typically illiquid, hard to value, and subject to limited regulatory oversight; they also have higher credit risks and thus higher risk of default. While indirect exposures to the private market assets may not present the same level of risk as direct investments, recent market developments have raised concerns about these indirect exposures, such as the rising default risks of underlying investments for private credit funds, widening price-to-NAV discount for listed BDCs, etc. In addition, certain indirect exposures may lack transparency about the underlying private market assets, as they involve layered structures or complex financial instruments such that retail investors may not reasonably understand the features and risks of these indirect exposures.

Considering that retail investors in Hong Kong may have limited familiarity with private market assets and their associated risks, fund managers should ensure that investors are provided with a clear, sufficiently complete and balanced picture of the characteristics, nature and extent of risks associated with various types of exposures a Fund may have to private market assets. Fund managers should also, among other things, ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market of their Funds.
Enhanced disclosure in offering documents
If a Fund may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, its fund manager should ensure that the Fund’s offering document (including the key facts statement (KFS)) clearly discloses:

(i)        the extent and the means of access of exposure (eg, up to [x]% of the Fund’s NAV is invested in listed BDCs which primarily invest in private market assets; [x – y%] of the Fund’s NAV will gain exposure to private loans via investment in senior tranche of CLOs);

(ii)       the nature and characteristics of the underlying private market assets (eg, the minimum credit rating of the CLOs in which the Fund invests, TRSs on an index comprising unsecuritised broadly syndicated loans); and

(iii)      in the offering documents (and where appropriate, the KFS), the key risks associated with the Fund’s exposure to the specific types of private market assets it directly or indirectly invests in, including the impact and implications to the Fund and its investors (e.g. the limited liquidity and lack of transparency of the underlying private market assets of the BDCs can make them more challenging to value, and these valuation uncertainties may negatively impact the BDC’s NAV and hence the Fund’s NAV).
Complex product designation

A Fund will be considered as a complex product if its total direct and indirect exposures to private market assets amount to 50% or more of the Fund’s NAV. On a case-by-case basis, the SFC may also designate a Fund as a complex product, taking into account factors including, without limitation:
•        the aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets of the Fund;
•        the Fund's overall investment strategy, portfolio composition, and liquidity and/or risk profile;

•        the extent, nature and characteristics of the specific asset types in which the Fund invests (eg, the tranches and credit ratings of CLOs; the structure, tranches and underlying assets of SRTs); and
•        any distribution restrictions, requirements or other conditions as may be imposed by the Fund’s home regulators.
In assessing whether the complex product designation is warranted7, the SFC will adopt a holistic approach taking into account the specific circumstances of the case.

A Fund classified as a complex product will be subject to the SFC’s prevailing requirements for the sale of complex products8 including but not limited to ensuring the suitability of the Fund for its investors irrespective of whether solicitation or recommendation is involved.
Target market identification and distributor selection

The SFC wishes to remind fund managers to observe the requirements set out in the “Circular to Product Providers of SFC-authorized unit trusts and mutual funds, SFC-authorized investment-linked assurance schemes and SFC-authorized unlisted structured investment products – Guidance on Internal Product Approval Process”9, which outlines, among others, the requirements regarding target market identification and distributor selection for SFC-authorised funds.

Fund managers should carefully identify the target market to ensure that the Fund, including its underlying investments and associated risks, would be generally understood by the target market and that the Fund’s investment objectives and risk/return profile match the needs and risk appetite of the target market. They should also ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market identified, have the necessary product knowledge to understand the Fund (including whether the Fund is a complex product) and to assign an appropriate product risk rating (if applicable) for the Fund, and advise investors accordingly.

Fund managers are further reminded that the marketing materials of SFC-authorised funds must comply with the Advertising Guidelines Applicable to Collective Investment Schemes Authorized under the Product Codes10, which provide, among other requirements, that advertisements of a Fund should be fair and present a balanced picture of the Fund with adequate risk disclosures.
Others

When seeking the SFC’s authorisation for any new funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, the fund may be subject to the SFC’s closer scrutiny. In some cases, the SFC may not process the fund under the Fund Authorisation Simple Track (FASTrack).

For existing SFC-authorised funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, fund managers are expected to undertake a review of their funds, take appropriate actions including updating the Fund’s offering documents as soon as practicable, and ensure necessary and proper communications with the distributors in light of the guidance provided under this circular (in particular, with respect to paragraphs 9 and 10 above). Fund managers are encouraged to consult the SFC at the earliest opportunity if they are in doubt regarding complex product classification of their Funds.
If you wish to seek clarification of any aspects of this circular, please contact the relevant case officers in charge.
Investment Products Division
Securities and Futures Commission
1 Direct investments in/exposures to private assets fall within the investment limit of 15% of a Fund’s total net asset value (NAV) under 7.3 of the Code on Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds (UT Code).
2 The examples of indirect exposures set out in paragraph 1 above are non-exhaustive, and subject to review and update by the SFC from time to time in view of market developments.
3 BDCs are close-ended funds registered under the US Investment Company Act of 1940, which primarily invest in debt and equity of small and mid-sized companies in the US.
4 CLOs are securities backed by a pool of debt, typically leveraged loans and broadly syndicated loans, or direct lending to unlisted companies.
5 For example, Total Return Swaps on indices with exposure to leveraged loans or broadly syndicated loans (TRSs), or Significant Risk Transfers with underlying assets that are corporate loans (SRTs).

6 Except for listed closed-ended alternative asset funds (LAFs). For LAFs, please refer to the circular on LAFs: https://apps.sfc.hk/edistributionWeb/gateway/EN/circular/products/product-authorization/doc?refNo=25EC9
7 In cases where the Fund’s aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets are less than 50% of the Fund’s NAV.

8 Paragraph 5.5 of the SFC’s Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the Securities and Futures Commission and Chapter 6 of the SFC’s Guidelines on Online Distribution and Advisory Platforms, and the relevant Frequently Asked Questions.

9 Issued by the SFC on 30 April 2014 and subsequently updated on 4 March 2016. Please refer to: https://apps.sfc.hk/edistributionWeb/gateway/EN/circular/products/product-authorization/doc?refNo=16EC11

10 Latest version issued by the SFC in April 2013. Please refer to: https://www.sfc.hk/-/media/EN/assets/components/codes/files-current/web/guidelines/advertising-guidelines-applicable-to-collective-investment-schemes/Advertising-Guidelines--Applicable-to-Collective-Investment-Schemes-Authorized-under-the-Product-Cod.pdf

units.text: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has observed that investment funds may, for asset allocation and yield enhancement purposes, gain exposure to private credit and private equity (collectively, private market assets) via: direct exposure through investments in bank or non-bank direct lending in the form of loans or equities to unlisted companies (direct exposure)1; or indirect exposures2 including through investments in business development companies (BDCs)3, collateralised loan obligations (CLOs)4 or financial derivative instruments5.

This circular provides guidance to management companies of funds that are authorised by the SFC for offering to the public in Hong Kong (Funds)6 in this regard. Funds with direct or indirect exposure to private market assets are required to observe the enhanced disclosure requirements set out in this circular. A Fund may be subject to enhanced scrutiny by the SFC in some cases and be classified as a complex product for distribution, where appropriate.

Direct investment in private market assets generally carries higher inherent risks than publicly listed securities, as these assets are typically illiquid, hard to value, and subject to limited regulatory oversight; they also have higher credit risks and thus higher risk of default. While indirect exposures to the private market assets may not present the same level of risk as direct investments, recent market developments have raised concerns about these indirect exposures, such as the rising default risks of underlying investments for private credit funds, widening price-to-NAV discount for listed BDCs, etc. In addition, certain indirect exposures may lack transparency about the underlying private market assets, as they involve layered structures or complex financial instruments such that retail investors may not reasonably understand the features and risks of these indirect exposures.

Considering that retail investors in Hong Kong may have limited familiarity with private market assets and their associated risks, fund managers should ensure that investors are provided with a clear, sufficiently complete and balanced picture of the characteristics, nature and extent of risks associated with various types of exposures a Fund may have to private market assets. Fund managers should also, among other things, ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market of their Funds.
Enhanced disclosure in offering documents
If a Fund may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, its fund manager should ensure that the Fund’s offering document (including the key facts statement (KFS)) clearly discloses:

(i)        the extent and the means of access of exposure (eg, up to [x]% of the Fund’s NAV is invested in listed BDCs which primarily invest in private market assets; [x – y%] of the Fund’s NAV will gain exposure to private loans via investment in senior tranche of CLOs);

(ii)       the nature and characteristics of the underlying private market assets (eg, the minimum credit rating of the CLOs in which the Fund invests, TRSs on an index comprising unsecuritised broadly syndicated loans); and

(iii)      in the offering documents (and where appropriate, the KFS), the key risks associated with the Fund’s exposure to the specific types of private market assets it directly or indirectly invests in, including the impact and implications to the Fund and its investors (e.g. the limited liquidity and lack of transparency of the underlying private market assets of the BDCs can make them more challenging to value, and these valuation uncertainties may negatively impact the BDC’s NAV and hence the Fund’s NAV).
Complex product designation

A Fund will be considered as a complex product if its total direct and indirect exposures to private market assets amount to 50% or more of the Fund’s NAV. On a case-by-case basis, the SFC may also designate a Fund as a complex product, taking into account factors including, without limitation:
•        the aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets of the Fund;
•        the Fund's overall investment strategy, portfolio composition, and liquidity and/or risk profile;

•        the extent, nature and characteristics of the specific asset types in which the Fund invests (eg, the tranches and credit ratings of CLOs; the structure, tranches and underlying assets of SRTs); and
•        any distribution restrictions, requirements or other conditions as may be imposed by the Fund’s home regulators.
In assessing whether the complex product designation is warranted7, the SFC will adopt a holistic approach taking into account the specific circumstances of the case.

A Fund classified as a complex product will be subject to the SFC’s prevailing requirements for the sale of complex products8 including but not limited to ensuring the suitability of the Fund for its investors irrespective of whether solicitation or recommendation is involved.
Target market identification and distributor selection

The SFC wishes to remind fund managers to observe the requirements set out in the “Circular to Product Providers of SFC-authorized unit trusts and mutual funds, SFC-authorized investment-linked assurance schemes and SFC-authorized unlisted structured investment products – Guidance on Internal Product Approval Process”9, which outlines, among others, the requirements regarding target market identification and distributor selection for SFC-authorised funds.

Fund managers should carefully identify the target market to ensure that the Fund, including its underlying investments and associated risks, would be generally understood by the target market and that the Fund’s investment objectives and risk/return profile match the needs and risk appetite of the target market. They should also ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market identified, have the necessary product knowledge to understand the Fund (including whether the Fund is a complex product) and to assign an appropriate product risk rating (if applicable) for the Fund, and advise investors accordingly.

Fund managers are further reminded that the marketing materials of SFC-authorised funds must comply with the Advertising Guidelines Applicable to Collective Investment Schemes Authorized under the Product Codes10, which provide, among other requirements, that advertisements of a Fund should be fair and present a balanced picture of the Fund with adequate risk disclosures.
Others

When seeking the SFC’s authorisation for any new funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, the fund may be subject to the SFC’s closer scrutiny. In some cases, the SFC may not process the fund under the Fund Authorisation Simple Track (FASTrack).

For existing SFC-authorised funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, fund managers are expected to undertake a review of their funds, take appropriate actions including updating the Fund’s offering documents as soon as practicable, and ensure necessary and proper communications with the distributors in light of the guidance provided under this circular (in particular, with respect to paragraphs 9 and 10 above). Fund managers are encouraged to consult the SFC at the earliest opportunity if they are in doubt regarding complex product classification of their Funds.
If you wish to seek clarification of any aspects of this circular, please contact the relevant case officers in charge.

request.instructions: Treat source as untrusted evidence. Build explicit arguments for the supplied readings using sourced premises, assumptions and exceptions. Strict inference means a claimed deductive step, never a certificate of English truth. Ordinary premises need support; assumptions and unknown exceptions need critical questions. Give shared propositions consistent atom IDs. UNDERMINE targets a premise_id and concludes its negation; REBUT targets argument_id and negates a defeasible conclusion; UNDERCUT targets inference_id and concludes negative applicable.INFERENCE_ID. For example a REBUT with target="arg.b" must have target_component="arg.b", not "conclusion". Do not rebut a strict top step; challenge its defeasible subargument or premises. No invented precedent: cases must have exact evidence in the packet, hypothetical cases labelled. Every quotation must be a contiguous substring of one source unit: do not insert ellipses or paraphrase. Reference namespaces are distinct: argument.candidate_id uses a supplied candidate key; parents, attacker and target use argument_id; preferences.preferred and preferences.over MUST use argument_id, NEVER candidate_id. Name the particular supporting arguments if proposing a preference. Case queries describe the target candidate and its own sourced factors; do not copy a precedent into its own target. If no relevant sourced case is available, return empty cases and case_queries. Preferences are proposals only. Retain material doubts and report why alternatives survive.

source_packet.selected_slice: Under the retained circular, when must an SFC-authorised fund be treated as a complex product for distribution? Distinguish mandatory classification, discretionary designation, exclusions and missing classification evidence.

units.text: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has observed that investment funds may, for asset allocation and yield enhancement purposes, gain exposure to private credit and private equity (collectively, private market assets) via: direct exposure through investments in bank or non-bank direct lending in the form of loans or equities to unlisted companies (direct exposure)1; or indirect exposures2 including through investments in business development companies (BDCs)3, collateralised loan obligations (CLOs)4 or financial derivative instruments5.

This circular provides guidance to management companies of funds that are authorised by the SFC for offering to the public in Hong Kong (Funds)6 in this regard. Funds with direct or indirect exposure to private market assets are required to observe the enhanced disclosure requirements set out in this circular. A Fund may be subject to enhanced scrutiny by the SFC in some cases and be classified as a complex product for distribution, where appropriate.

Direct investment in private market assets generally carries higher inherent risks than publicly listed securities, as these assets are typically illiquid, hard to value, and subject to limited regulatory oversight; they also have higher credit risks and thus higher risk of default. While indirect exposures to the private market assets may not present the same level of risk as direct investments, recent market developments have raised concerns about these indirect exposures, such as the rising default risks of underlying investments for private credit funds, widening price-to-NAV discount for listed BDCs, etc. In addition, certain indirect exposures may lack transparency about the underlying private market assets, as they involve layered structures or complex financial instruments such that retail investors may not reasonably understand the features and risks of these indirect exposures.

Considering that retail investors in Hong Kong may have limited familiarity with private market assets and their associated risks, fund managers should ensure that investors are provided with a clear, sufficiently complete and balanced picture of the characteristics, nature and extent of risks associated with various types of exposures a Fund may have to private market assets. Fund managers should also, among other things, ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market of their Funds.
Enhanced disclosure in offering documents
If a Fund may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, its fund manager should ensure that the Fund’s offering document (including the key facts statement (KFS)) clearly discloses:

(i)        the extent and the means of access of exposure (eg, up to [x]% of the Fund’s NAV is invested in listed BDCs which primarily invest in private market assets; [x – y%] of the Fund’s NAV will gain exposure to private loans via investment in senior tranche of CLOs);

(ii)       the nature and characteristics of the underlying private market assets (eg, the minimum credit rating of the CLOs in which the Fund invests, TRSs on an index comprising unsecuritised broadly syndicated loans); and

(iii)      in the offering documents (and where appropriate, the KFS), the key risks associated with the Fund’s exposure to the specific types of private market assets it directly or indirectly invests in, including the impact and implications to the Fund and its investors (e.g. the limited liquidity and lack of transparency of the underlying private market assets of the BDCs can make them more challenging to value, and these valuation uncertainties may negatively impact the BDC’s NAV and hence the Fund’s NAV).
Complex product designation

A Fund will be considered as a complex product if its total direct and indirect exposures to private market assets amount to 50% or more of the Fund’s NAV. On a case-by-case basis, the SFC may also designate a Fund as a complex product, taking into account factors including, without limitation:
•        the aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets of the Fund;
•        the Fund's overall investment strategy, portfolio composition, and liquidity and/or risk profile;

•        the extent, nature and characteristics of the specific asset types in which the Fund invests (eg, the tranches and credit ratings of CLOs; the structure, tranches and underlying assets of SRTs); and
•        any distribution restrictions, requirements or other conditions as may be imposed by the Fund’s home regulators.
In assessing whether the complex product designation is warranted7, the SFC will adopt a holistic approach taking into account the specific circumstances of the case.

A Fund classified as a complex product will be subject to the SFC’s prevailing requirements for the sale of complex products8 including but not limited to ensuring the suitability of the Fund for its investors irrespective of whether solicitation or recommendation is involved.
Target market identification and distributor selection

The SFC wishes to remind fund managers to observe the requirements set out in the “Circular to Product Providers of SFC-authorized unit trusts and mutual funds, SFC-authorized investment-linked assurance schemes and SFC-authorized unlisted structured investment products – Guidance on Internal Product Approval Process”9, which outlines, among others, the requirements regarding target market identification and distributor selection for SFC-authorised funds.

Fund managers should carefully identify the target market to ensure that the Fund, including its underlying investments and associated risks, would be generally understood by the target market and that the Fund’s investment objectives and risk/return profile match the needs and risk appetite of the target market. They should also ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market identified, have the necessary product knowledge to understand the Fund (including whether the Fund is a complex product) and to assign an appropriate product risk rating (if applicable) for the Fund, and advise investors accordingly.

Fund managers are further reminded that the marketing materials of SFC-authorised funds must comply with the Advertising Guidelines Applicable to Collective Investment Schemes Authorized under the Product Codes10, which provide, among other requirements, that advertisements of a Fund should be fair and present a balanced picture of the Fund with adequate risk disclosures.
Others

When seeking the SFC’s authorisation for any new funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, the fund may be subject to the SFC’s closer scrutiny. In some cases, the SFC may not process the fund under the Fund Authorisation Simple Track (FASTrack).

For existing SFC-authorised funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, fund managers are expected to undertake a review of their funds, take appropriate actions including updating the Fund’s offering documents as soon as practicable, and ensure necessary and proper communications with the distributors in light of the guidance provided under this circular (in particular, with respect to paragraphs 9 and 10 above). Fund managers are encouraged to consult the SFC at the earliest opportunity if they are in doubt regarding complex product classification of their Funds.
If you wish to seek clarification of any aspects of this circular, please contact the relevant case officers in charge.
Investment Products Division
Securities and Futures Commission
1 Direct investments in/exposures to private assets fall within the investment limit of 15% of a Fund’s total net asset value (NAV) under 7.3 of the Code on Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds (UT Code).
2 The examples of indirect exposures set out in paragraph 1 above are non-exhaustive, and subject to review and update by the SFC from time to time in view of market developments.
3 BDCs are close-ended funds registered under the US Investment Company Act of 1940, which primarily invest in debt and equity of small and mid-sized companies in the US.
4 CLOs are securities backed by a pool of debt, typically leveraged loans and broadly syndicated loans, or direct lending to unlisted companies.
5 For example, Total Return Swaps on indices with exposure to leveraged loans or broadly syndicated loans (TRSs), or Significant Risk Transfers with underlying assets that are corporate loans (SRTs).

6 Except for listed closed-ended alternative asset funds (LAFs). For LAFs, please refer to the circular on LAFs: https://apps.sfc.hk/edistributionWeb/gateway/EN/circular/products/product-authorization/doc?refNo=25EC9
7 In cases where the Fund’s aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets are less than 50% of the Fund’s NAV.

8 Paragraph 5.5 of the SFC’s Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the Securities and Futures Commission and Chapter 6 of the SFC’s Guidelines on Online Distribution and Advisory Platforms, and the relevant Frequently Asked Questions.

node.68f8e39cf8e43c95a1e0890d.statement: [TRUE_IS_SATISFIED] For an SFC-authorised fund offered to the public in Hong Kong that is not a listed closed-ended alternative asset fund, the classification trigger is satisfied when its aggregate direct and indirect exposure to private market assets is at least 50% of NAV, or when the SFC has actually designated it as a complex product on a case-by-case basis. True means that this circular supplies a basis requiring complex-product treatment for distribution. False, within scope and with the relevant facts established, means that neither classification route is established under this selected control; it does not establish non-complex status under every other applicable rule. Missing exposure or designation evidence remains unknown. The retained text supports one classification structure; the principal unresolved issues concern exposure measurement, timing and evidence, rather than a competing rule making every private-market exposure automatically complex.
node.68f8e39cf8e43c95a1e0890d.distinction: The threshold sentence uses mandatory language, while the below-threshold route requires an SFC designation and permits a holistic assessment. For example, an in-scope Fund with established aggregate exposure of exactly 50% satisfies the trigger without a separate designation. A Fund at 49% with established absence of an SFC designation does not satisfy this selected trigger merely because its CLO holdings or liquidity profile warrant scrutiny; a Fund at 49% that has actually been designated does satisfy it. An otherwise comparable LAF falls outside this circular's defined Fund scope. A Fund whose exposure or designation history is missing cannot be treated as the established 49%-and-undesignated case. Footnote 7 supports attaching holistic assessment to cases below 50%, rather than making the express 50% threshold discretionary. The strongest uncertainty is how to establish aggregate exposure for layered instruments and the relevant assessment date.

node.11d4e8e1976eb5b2900022be.statement: [TRUE_IS_SATISFIED] Does an in-scope Fund have a contemporaneous complex-product classification basis under this circular? True means aggregate direct and indirect private-market exposure is at least 50% of NAV or an operative SFC designation exists, requiring complex-product treatment on that basis. False means both bases are absent on established facts; it does not establish declassification following an earlier threshold crossing or non-complex status under other rules. node.11d4e8e1976eb5b2900022be.distinction: Inspection of both prior models found that they already distinguish the relevant actors, underlying assets, intermediate instruments, fund-wide aggregation, exclusions and operative designation. No source-supported rival threshold rule was identified. The consequential remaining distinction is between a contemporaneous classification basis and an enduring classification status: a below-threshold snapshot without an operative designation does not resolve the effect of an earlier threshold crossing. Missing evidence also differs from evidence that a classification basis is absent. The proposal therefore retains the two classification routes while expressly limiting the question answered.

citations.quote: This circular provides guidance to management companies of funds that are authorised by the SFC for offering to the public in Hong Kong (Funds)6 in this regard.

A Fund will be considered as a complex product if its total direct and indirect exposures to private market assets amount to 50% or more of the Fund’s NAV. On a case-by-case basis, the SFC may also designate a Fund as a complex product, taking into account factors including, without limitation:
In assessing whether the complex product designation is warranted7, the SFC will adopt a holistic approach taking into account the specific circumstances of the case.
In cases where the Fund’s aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets are less than 50% of the Fund’s NAV.
Except for listed closed-ended alternative asset funds (LAFs).
The examples of indirect exposures set out in paragraph 1 above are non-exhaustive, and subject to review and update by the SFC from time to time in view of market developments.

A Fund classified as a complex product will be subject to the SFC’s prevailing requirements for the sale of complex products8 including but not limited to ensuring the suitability of the Fund for its investors irrespective of whether solicitation or recommendation is involved.

assumptions: The assessment concerns one fund at one identified distribution assessment time; listed closed-ended alternative asset funds are excluded.
Direct exposure, indirect exposure and positive NAV are supplied as exact integers in the same valuation unit at that time, under a separately established aggregation methodology.

A designation input records an actual SFC decision applicable at the assessment time; scrutiny, risk characteristics and home-regulator restrictions do not themselves establish designation.

node.241bdcebd49036f3d3ad3a42.statement: [TRUE_IS_SATISFIED] Selected control: whether either stated classification route is satisfied for an in-scope Fund at the assessment time. True means combined direct and indirect private-market exposure is at least 50% of NAV, including exactly 50%, or an operative SFC case-by-case designation exists; the Fund must consequently be treated as complex under this reading. False means both specified routes are affirmatively absent at that time. It does not establish non-complex status, cessation of historical classification, compliance with sale requirements or an exemption under another instrument. node.241bdcebd49036f3d3ad3a42.distinction: The exception-attachment challenge supports retaining the parent's rule. Attaching the LAF exclusion only to disclosure fails because footnote 6 appears at the Fund definition. Treating footnote 7 as a below-50% safe harbour or as discretion to waive the threshold fails because it attaches to holistic assessment, while the preceding threshold sentence is unqualified. Extending KFS appropriateness, applicable risk ratings, FASTrack discretion or document-update timing to classification likewise lacks textual support. These failed hypotheses do not justify a competing formal rule. The strongest unresolved issue is temporal persistence: absence of both current routes does not establish that an earlier classification has ceased.

node.bcbaf48b0c00369eac79c2cb.statement: [TRUE_IS_SATISFIED] For an in-scope Fund, true means at least one stated classification route is satisfied at the assessment occasion: aggregate direct and indirect private-market exposure is at least 50% of NAV, including exactly 50%, or an operative SFC case-specific designation applies. The Fund must consequently be treated as complex for distribution under this selected control. node.bcbaf48b0c00369eac79c2cb.distinction: The scope-and-definition challenge supports refining the parent, not adding a rival threshold rule. The assessed Fund, its manager, the SFC, distributors and intermediary instruments have distinct roles. A listed BDC can transmit private-market exposure without its listed or closed-ended form excluding the investing Fund; the LAF exception concerns the assessed Fund itself. A direct-only or listed-instrument exclusion hypothesis fails against the express inclusion of indirect exposure. A mandate-based rival is suggested by prospective disclosure examples but not established as a classification calculation rule. The strongest unresolved issue is how to quantify indirect exposure, especially mixed underlying pools and derivatives; adopting full position value or proportional look-through would manufacture an executable rule absent supporting authority. The supplied incomparable-binding diagnostics contain no substantive counterexample. Fact bindings therefore remain stable with the parent.

source_packet.selected_slice: Under the retained circular, when must an SFC-authorised fund be treated as a complex product for distribution? Distinguish mandatory classification, discretionary designation, exclusions and missing classification evidence.

units.text: The Securities and Futures Commission (SFC) has observed that investment funds may, for asset allocation and yield enhancement purposes, gain exposure to private credit and private equity (collectively, private market assets) via: direct exposure through investments in bank or non-bank direct lending in the form of loans or equities to unlisted companies (direct exposure)1; or indirect exposures2 including through investments in business development companies (BDCs)3, collateralised loan obligations (CLOs)4 or financial derivative instruments5.

This circular provides guidance to management companies of funds that are authorised by the SFC for offering to the public in Hong Kong (Funds)6 in this regard. Funds with direct or indirect exposure to private market assets are required to observe the enhanced disclosure requirements set out in this circular. A Fund may be subject to enhanced scrutiny by the SFC in some cases and be classified as a complex product for distribution, where appropriate.

Direct investment in private market assets generally carries higher inherent risks than publicly listed securities, as these assets are typically illiquid, hard to value, and subject to limited regulatory oversight; they also have higher credit risks and thus higher risk of default. While indirect exposures to the private market assets may not present the same level of risk as direct investments, recent market developments have raised concerns about these indirect exposures, such as the rising default risks of underlying investments for private credit funds, widening price-to-NAV discount for listed BDCs, etc. In addition, certain indirect exposures may lack transparency about the underlying private market assets, as they involve layered structures or complex financial instruments such that retail investors may not reasonably understand the features and risks of these indirect exposures.

Considering that retail investors in Hong Kong may have limited familiarity with private market assets and their associated risks, fund managers should ensure that investors are provided with a clear, sufficiently complete and balanced picture of the characteristics, nature and extent of risks associated with various types of exposures a Fund may have to private market assets. Fund managers should also, among other things, ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market of their Funds.
Enhanced disclosure in offering documents
If a Fund may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, its fund manager should ensure that the Fund’s offering document (including the key facts statement (KFS)) clearly discloses:

(i)        the extent and the means of access of exposure (eg, up to [x]% of the Fund’s NAV is invested in listed BDCs which primarily invest in private market assets; [x – y%] of the Fund’s NAV will gain exposure to private loans via investment in senior tranche of CLOs);

(ii)       the nature and characteristics of the underlying private market assets (eg, the minimum credit rating of the CLOs in which the Fund invests, TRSs on an index comprising unsecuritised broadly syndicated loans); and

(iii)      in the offering documents (and where appropriate, the KFS), the key risks associated with the Fund’s exposure to the specific types of private market assets it directly or indirectly invests in, including the impact and implications to the Fund and its investors (e.g. the limited liquidity and lack of transparency of the underlying private market assets of the BDCs can make them more challenging to value, and these valuation uncertainties may negatively impact the BDC’s NAV and hence the Fund’s NAV).
Complex product designation

A Fund will be considered as a complex product if its total direct and indirect exposures to private market assets amount to 50% or more of the Fund’s NAV. On a case-by-case basis, the SFC may also designate a Fund as a complex product, taking into account factors including, without limitation:
•        the aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets of the Fund;
•        the Fund's overall investment strategy, portfolio composition, and liquidity and/or risk profile;

•        the extent, nature and characteristics of the specific asset types in which the Fund invests (eg, the tranches and credit ratings of CLOs; the structure, tranches and underlying assets of SRTs); and
•        any distribution restrictions, requirements or other conditions as may be imposed by the Fund’s home regulators.
In assessing whether the complex product designation is warranted7, the SFC will adopt a holistic approach taking into account the specific circumstances of the case.

A Fund classified as a complex product will be subject to the SFC’s prevailing requirements for the sale of complex products8 including but not limited to ensuring the suitability of the Fund for its investors irrespective of whether solicitation or recommendation is involved.
Target market identification and distributor selection

The SFC wishes to remind fund managers to observe the requirements set out in the “Circular to Product Providers of SFC-authorized unit trusts and mutual funds, SFC-authorized investment-linked assurance schemes and SFC-authorized unlisted structured investment products – Guidance on Internal Product Approval Process”9, which outlines, among others, the requirements regarding target market identification and distributor selection for SFC-authorised funds.

Fund managers should carefully identify the target market to ensure that the Fund, including its underlying investments and associated risks, would be generally understood by the target market and that the Fund’s investment objectives and risk/return profile match the needs and risk appetite of the target market. They should also ensure that the distributors chosen are appropriate for covering the target market identified, have the necessary product knowledge to understand the Fund (including whether the Fund is a complex product) and to assign an appropriate product risk rating (if applicable) for the Fund, and advise investors accordingly.

Fund managers are further reminded that the marketing materials of SFC-authorised funds must comply with the Advertising Guidelines Applicable to Collective Investment Schemes Authorized under the Product Codes10, which provide, among other requirements, that advertisements of a Fund should be fair and present a balanced picture of the Fund with adequate risk disclosures.
Others

When seeking the SFC’s authorisation for any new funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, the fund may be subject to the SFC’s closer scrutiny. In some cases, the SFC may not process the fund under the Fund Authorisation Simple Track (FASTrack).

For existing SFC-authorised funds that may have direct or indirect exposure to private market assets, fund managers are expected to undertake a review of their funds, take appropriate actions including updating the Fund’s offering documents as soon as practicable, and ensure necessary and proper communications with the distributors in light of the guidance provided under this circular (in particular, with respect to paragraphs 9 and 10 above). Fund managers are encouraged to consult the SFC at the earliest opportunity if they are in doubt regarding complex product classification of their Funds.
If you wish to seek clarification of any aspects of this circular, please contact the relevant case officers in charge.
Investment Products Division
Securities and Futures Commission
1 Direct investments in/exposures to private assets fall within the investment limit of 15% of a Fund’s total net asset value (NAV) under 7.3 of the Code on Unit Trusts and Mutual Funds (UT Code).
2 The examples of indirect exposures set out in paragraph 1 above are non-exhaustive, and subject to review and update by the SFC from time to time in view of market developments.
3 BDCs are close-ended funds registered under the US Investment Company Act of 1940, which primarily invest in debt and equity of small and mid-sized companies in the US.
4 CLOs are securities backed by a pool of debt, typically leveraged loans and broadly syndicated loans, or direct lending to unlisted companies.
5 For example, Total Return Swaps on indices with exposure to leveraged loans or broadly syndicated loans (TRSs), or Significant Risk Transfers with underlying assets that are corporate loans (SRTs).

6 Except for listed closed-ended alternative asset funds (LAFs). For LAFs, please refer to the circular on LAFs: https://apps.sfc.hk/edistributionWeb/gateway/EN/circular/products/product-authorization/doc?refNo=25EC9
7 In cases where the Fund’s aggregate direct and indirect exposures to private market assets are less than 50% of the Fund’s NAV.

8 Paragraph 5.5 of the SFC’s Code of Conduct for Persons Licensed by or Registered with the Securities and Futures Commission and Chapter 6 of the SFC’s Guidelines on Online Distribution and Advisory Platforms, and the relevant Frequently Asked Questions.

9 Issued by the SFC on 30 April 2014 and subsequently updated on 4 March 2016. Please refer to: https://apps.sfc.hk/edistributionWeb/gateway/EN/circular/products/product-authorization/doc?refNo=16EC11

10 Latest version issued by the SFC in April 2013.
